# Breaking Change Guidelines

A cross-surface definition of what counts as a breaking change and how to handle one. Applies across projects in this standards set; use [Classify the Deliverable First](#classify-the-deliverable-first) to work out which parts apply to what you're shipping. The CLI-specific version-bump table lives in [Versioning](versioning.md); this document is the general rule that table is an instance of.

## Scope

This definition applies to a supported release of a project, used in an environment or configuration the project actually expects. Outside that, changing behavior is not a breaking change under this definition:

- **Experimental or explicitly unstable features are excluded.** A feature marked experimental, alpha, or otherwise not yet stable carries no compatibility expectation — it can change or be removed between releases. If your project distinguishes an early-access tier that real users are already trying from a purely internal, not-yet-usable tier, the early-access tier is still worth a lighter response than a stable feature — usually just a release-note entry — even though it's excluded from the heavier remedies below. People are relying on it enough to notice.
- **Environments or configurations the project never expected to work are excluded.** If a topology, configuration, or combination was never something the project validated or claimed to support, a change that stops it from working is not a breaking change — it was never a promise to begin with. Check your project's own documentation for what's expected or known-good; there's often no single authoritative list, so use judgment.
- **Internal-only interfaces stay internal, with no gray zone.** An interface is internal only as long as nothing outside the owning team depends on it. The moment an external consumer depends on it, it is not internal anymore, by definition, and the rest of this document applies to it like any other surface — don't keep calling something "internal" to excuse it from rules it no longer qualifies for. A genuinely internal interface carries no external compatibility obligation and needs no deprecation cycle.

  This does not make a genuinely internal interface risk-free, though: it is still in scope for [Mixed-Version Coexistence](#mixed-version-coexistence-deployedha-services-only). During a rolling upgrade, a workload still running the old version can call an internal interface on a node that has already been upgraded, and vice versa. A change there can still break a user's running workload even though no external consumer ever calls the interface directly.

When a change sits near one of these boundaries — a feature graduating out of experimental status, a configuration whose support status is unclear — treat it as in scope and raise it, rather than assuming the exclusion applies.

## Definition

A **breaking change** is any change that requires an existing consumer of a supported surface to take action it would not otherwise have needed to take, in order to keep working the way it did before.

"Consumer" is deliberately broad: an API client, a CLI script, a running deployment being upgraded, a dashboard or alert reading your metrics, a library depending on your exported symbols, a downstream service parsing your logs. If something out there depends on the current shape or behavior of a supported surface, changing that shape or behavior without a compatible path is breaking, regardless of which surface it happens on.

A **non-breaking change** is additive or corrective: it doesn't require a well-behaved consumer (see [Assumption: Clients Tolerate Additive Change](#assumption-clients-tolerate-additive-change) below) to change anything.

## Assumption: Clients Tolerate Additive Change

Everything in this document assumes consumers hold up their end: they ignore unknown response fields and handle unrecognized enum/variant values gracefully rather than failing on them. This is asserted up front as a baseline expectation for every surface in scope, not something each team re-derives case by case.

Without this assumption, adding an optional field or a new enum value would itself be breaking for any consumer that rejects unrecognized data — non-breaking evolution wouldn't be possible at all. If a known consumer can't meet this bar, treat additive changes to the surfaces it depends on as breaking for that consumer until it's fixed.

## Classify the Deliverable First

Not every facet below applies to every kind of thing you ship. Determine which of these the change lives in before judging it:

| Deliverable type | Signal | Facets that apply |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| **Batch tool / library** | No server process, no persisted state between invocations, imported/invoked and exits | Interface breaks only (API/CLI/exported symbols, config, schema) |
| **Long-running service, single instance** | Runs continuously, has persisted state or config, but only one version runs at a time | Interface breaks + persisted-state/migration safety in both upgrade directions |
| **Deployed / HA service** | Rolling upgrades, multiple replicas, or a supported upgrade path across environments (Dockerfile, k8s/helm manifests, operator manifests, migration directories are evidence) | All of the above, plus mixed-version coexistence, in-flight work surviving the upgrade, and rollback |

Reviewing a batch tool for "does an in-flight workflow survive a rolling upgrade" is a false positive — that facet is N/A. Reviewing a deployed HA service and skipping rollback because "it's just a schema change" is a false negative. Most projects in this standards set are batch tools or libraries — the persisted-state and mixed-version facets below rarely apply, but check before assuming.

## Surface Areas

Breaking-change rules apply to every interface a consumer can depend on, not only the API:

| Surface | Examples |
| :---- | :---- |
| **HTTP API** | Endpoint paths, URL structure, query/path parameters, request/response schemas, status codes, auth requirements |
| **CLI** | Command names, flag names and semantics, output format (human and machine-readable) |
| **Data schema** | Database tables/columns, migration sequencing, stored object shapes |
| **Declarative resources** | Operator CRs, config-as-code formats, other spec-driven resources |
| **Configuration** | Env vars, config file keys, defaults |
| **Operational surfaces** | Metric names and labels, log field names/formats, trace attributes |
| **Behavioral** | Execution semantics, ordering, defaults applied at runtime — even with no interface change |
| **UI routes** | Page URLs, deep links |
| **Third-party integrations** | Auth app registration, external URL callbacks, anything a separately-lifecycled app depends on |

Operational surfaces belong on this list for a concrete reason: a metric or log field rename breaks a dashboard or alert exactly the way a response field rename breaks an API client. Nobody reviews it that way by default, which is why it's called out explicitly.

## URL Structure Is Part of the Interface

Renaming, moving, or restructuring a URL path is breaking, even when the response body is unchanged — clients hardcode paths, not just field names. The same applies to query and path parameters: renaming a parameter, changing what values it accepts, or making an optional parameter required is breaking under the same rules as a request body field. Adding a new optional parameter is not. The same logic applies to CLI subcommands — see [Versioning](versioning.md).

This applies to UI routes as much as API paths. A bookmarked page, a shared link, a deep link from documentation or a support ticket, a browser history entry — all depend on the URL staying stable, not on any code calling it. Changing a page's URL is breaking by the same logic as changing an API endpoint's path, whether or not anything programmatic is involved. Reorganizing navigation without changing the URL (moving a menu item, relabeling a page) is not breaking under this definition — nothing depended on where the entry point into an unchanged URL was. Changes to DOM structure or element selectors are a separate, narrower case: not breaking for human users, but breaking for anything automated that depends on them (e2e test suites, RPA tools).

## The Directionality Rule

For any interface with an accepted-input side and a produced-output side, the general rule is:

- **Narrowing what you accept is breaking.** Requiring a previously optional input, rejecting a previously accepted value, tightening validation.
- **Widening what you produce is breaking.** A response field becoming nullable when it wasn't, a return type gaining new possible shapes an existing consumer didn't code for.
- **Widening what you accept, and/or narrowing what you produce (in ways consumers already tolerate), is safe.** Adding an optional field, adding an enum value a well-behaved consumer already ignores.

## A Breaking Change Without Its Required Signal Is Itself a Finding

This applies to surfaces that are versioned, can reasonably be versioned, or are otherwise expected to carry an explicit compatibility signal — APIs, CLIs, CRDs, and other declarative specs. It doesn't apply the same way to surfaces that aren't versioned and can't reasonably be: UI, logs, and metrics don't carry version numbers, so a breaking change there isn't missing "a version bump" — it's missing whatever signal that surface's remedy calls for instead (see [The Remedy Isn't the Same for Every Surface](#the-remedy-isnt-the-same-for-every-surface)).

For a versioned surface, a breaking change that isn't accompanied by a major version bump, a deprecation notice, or a migration note is a separate defect from the breaking change itself. Consumers can plan around a signaled break; they cannot plan around a silent one. When reviewing a change, the absence of the expected signal on an otherwise-justified breaking change is something to flag on its own, not something the breaking-change label alone covers.

## The Remedy Isn't the Same for Every Surface

Calling something a breaking change is a classification, not a plan. What it costs to ship it responsibly varies a lot by surface, and that cost is part of the decision to accept the change at all — not something to work out afterward.

| Surface | Typical remedy | Who signs off |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| API, CLI, declarative specs (CRDs, config-as-code) | Heaviest: new version alongside the old, old one deprecated and kept working for a defined window, migration guide | Surface owner, plus any API/spec governance your project has |
| Data schema / persisted state | Backward- and, where rollback is supported, forward-compatible migration for a defined window | Service owner |
| Operational surfaces (metrics, logs, traces) | Lighter: a changelog/release-note entry and direct coordination with whoever consumes the metric or log (dashboards, alerts). No mandated parallel-support window, but not a unilateral change either — the team depending on it needs a say. | Surface owner + consuming team |
| Deployment or upgrade behavior (HA, rolling upgrade) | Can be entirely procedural: a documented upgrade step (e.g. "drain in-flight work before upgrading") and a changelog entry, with no code-level coexistence mechanism at all | Release docs + ops |

The point of sorting a change into one of these rows before shipping it: a breaking change that needs a full version-deprecation cycle is a materially different call than one that needs a changelog line and a conversation with the team it affects. Treating them the same either over-invests in the cheap case or under-invests in the expensive one. For a single-maintainer CLI tool, "who signs off" collapses to "you, deliberately" — the point is still to make the call on purpose, not track it as an approval chain.

## What Is Not a Breaking Change

- Adding a new endpoint, command, field, enum value, or optional parameter
- Correcting a bug in behavior nobody could have been correctly relying on (document it in release notes regardless)
- Changing human-readable text (error messages, help text) where the structured error code/exit status is unchanged
- Data changes inside a field that was already documented as an open-ended map (e.g. user-supplied labels) — what's promised is the map's existence, not its current keys

## Persisted State and Migrations

For long-running and deployed services, compatibility runs in both directions: a migration must work going forward (existing data survives the upgrade) and, where rollback is supported, the previous version must still be able to read data written by the new one until the rollback window closes. A migration that silently drops or reshapes data with no rollback path is breaking even if no interface changed.

## Mixed-Version Coexistence (Deployed/HA Services Only)

During a rolling upgrade, old and new instances of a service may run simultaneously, and work in flight (a queued job, an open connection, a multi-step workflow) may start on one version and finish on another. A change that only works correctly when every instance is upgraded is breaking for any service that can't be upgraded atomically — which is most of them.

This applies to service-to-service calls as much as to work in flight. During a rolling upgrade, a workload still running the old version can call an internal interface on a node that has already been upgraded, and a new-version workload can just as easily call a node that hasn't rolled forward yet. Both directions have to keep working for the duration of the rollout. This is the concrete mechanism behind the internal-interface note in [Scope](#scope): the "consumer" of a purely internal interface, during the upgrade window, is your own previous or next release calling itself across the version boundary.

## Assessing a Change

**This section is a starting placeholder, not a finished rubric.** It sketches the questions to work through; it hasn't been through the same scrutiny as the rest of this document and will need revision.

1. **Which surface does the change touch?** Pick a row from [Surface Areas](#surface-areas). A change can touch more than one.
2. **Who is the consumer, and does it cross a version boundary?** External user/integration, internal-only, or a mixed-version internal call during a rolling upgrade (see [Mixed-Version Coexistence](#mixed-version-coexistence-deployedha-services-only))? Exposure changes which facets below apply — an internal-only change still needs the mixed-version check even with no external consumer.
3. **Is this surface versioned, or should it be?** If yes, does the change require a major version bump under [the directionality rule](#the-directionality-rule)? If the surface isn't versioned and can't reasonably be (UI, logs, metrics), skip the version-bump question and go straight to the remedy.
4. **Does this have to be delivered as a breaking change?** Before accepting the classification, ask whether an alternative delivery — additive-first sequencing, a setting, a smaller-scoped change, a versioned rollout — avoids breaking anything at all. If an alternative exists, weigh its cost against the cost of the breaking change (from the remedy table) and the value of avoiding the break. Record the answer and the reasoning somewhere durable — a linked issue or pull-request comment, or a decision captured in your project's own design docs — so "we considered a non-breaking path and chose not to take it" isn't lost to a merged PR.
5. **What does [the remedy table](#the-remedy-isnt-the-same-for-every-surface) require for this surface?** This determines the minimum acceptable handling — deprecation cycle, changelog entry, documented upgrade step, or some combination.
6. **Is there sign-off at the level the remedy requires?** Shipping the change means accepting its user-impact implications in the way it's being delivered. Confirm that sign-off exists at the right level before merging, not after.

Accepting a breaking change is not a binary "yes, it's breaking" — it's a decision that this breaking change, with its alternatives and their costs considered, is worth shipping this way. That decision needs a record, not just a merge.
